questions.q: Which rank comes directly between order and genus?
why: Step 1: write KPCOFGS — Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Step 2: find order (O) and genus (G).
Step 3: the letter between them is F → Family.
questions.tip: Write the mnemonic letters across the top of your answer sheet before you start.

similar.q: Which rank comes directly above class?
similar.a: Phylum.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Which scientific name is written correctly in print?
why: Step 1: genus needs a capital — rules out zea mays.
Step 2: species needs a small letter — rules out Zea Mays and ZEA MAYS.
Step 3: a printed name is in italics — *Zea mays* fits all rules.
questions.tip: Check three things in order: capital genus, small species, italics/underlining.

similar.q: How is *Acacia tortilis* written the second time in a text?
similar.a: *A. tortilis*.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: List the four rules for writing a scientific name.
questions.answer: 1) One organism has only one scientific name. 2) It has two parts: genus then species. 3) Genus begins with a capital letter, species with a small letter. 4) Italics when printed; genus and species underlined separately when handwritten.
why: Step 1: “one” — only one scientific name per organism.
Step 2: “two” — two parts, genus first, species second.
Step 3: “capital/small” — Genus capital, species small.
Step 4: “slanted or lined” — italics in print, separate underlines by hand.
questions.tip: Remember 1-2-Capital-Italics: one name, two parts, capital first, italics.

similar.q: Write the scientific name of the house fly correctly by hand and say how it is marked.
similar.a: *Musca domestica* — by hand, underline Musca and domestica separately.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Why do taxonomists avoid common names and use Latin?
questions.answer: Common names differ between languages and places, so they are not universal. Latin is no longer changing, so a Latin name is fixed and the same for scientists everywhere.
why: Step 1: a common name changes with language — lion is ኣንበሳ in Tigrinya, simba in Swahili.
Step 2: one organism could have many local names, and one name could mean different organisms.
Step 3: Latin does not change and is used by scientists everywhere → one fixed name worldwide.
questions.tip: Give an example with two languages — examiners like a concrete example.

similar.q: Why is the aloe found near Massawa called *Aloe massawana*?
similar.a: The place name was Latinised to make the species name.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Which statement about the hierarchy is correct?

options.A: Members of a kingdom are more alike than members of a genus
options.B: Moving from kingdom to species, groups get smaller and members more alike

why: Step 1: species is the smallest, most specific group.
Step 2: kingdom is the biggest, least specific group.
Step 3: so going down, size decreases and similarity increases → B.
Step 4: A, C and D reverse the order.
questions.tip: Draw the pyramid: wide top (kingdom), narrow bottom (species).

similar.q: Which group has more different kinds of organisms: a phylum or a family?
similar.a: A phylum — it is a higher rank and contains many families.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Classify a human up to species level.
questions.answer: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates, Family Hominidae, Genus *Homo*, Species *sapiens* — *Homo sapiens*.
why: Step 1: kingdom — multicellular, no cell wall, ingests food → Animalia.
Step 2: phylum — backbone → Chordata.
Step 3: class — hair, milk → Mammalia.
Step 4: order Primates, family Hominidae.
Step 5: genus *Homo*, species *sapiens*.
questions.tip: Say KPCOFGS aloud and fill one rank per step.

similar.q: Classify maize up to species level.
similar.a: Plantae, Angiospermae, Monocotyledon, Commelinales, Poaceae, *Zea*, *mays*.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Members of the same genus can always interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
why: Step 1: fertile offspring is the test for the **same species**.
Step 2: members of the same genus may interbreed, but the offspring may be infertile — the mule (horse × donkey).
Step 3: so the statement is false.
questions.tip: Mule = genus-level cross. Fertile = species.

similar.q: Can two members of the same species produce fertile offspring?
similar.a: Yes — that is what defines a species.

questions.label: 2.1 Practice

questions.q: Each pair of statements in a dichotomous key is called a
why: Step 1: dichotomous = cut into two.
Step 2: a pair of mutually exclusive statements = a couplet.
questions.tip: Couple = two → couplet.

similar.q: What does “mutually exclusive” mean in a key?
similar.a: Only one of the two statements can be true for the specimen.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

questions.q: Using the textbook key, an animal that is terrestrial, wingless, plant eating and has an undivided hoof is a
why: Couplet 1: terrestrial → 2.
Couplet 2: wingless → 3.
Couplet 3: plant eating → 4.
Couplet 4: undivided hoof → donkey.
questions.tip: Always start at couplet 1 and write the path (1→2→3→4).

similar.q: Which animal is terrestrial, wingless and flesh eating?
similar.a: Hyena.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

questions.q: Give the four steps for constructing a dichotomous key.
questions.answer: a) List the main features of the organisms, especially those that make each one unique. b) Arrange the features in pairs. c) For each pair, write either the organism’s name or the number of the next couplet. d) Continue until every organism is named.
why: Step 1: features first (observe).
Step 2: pair them as opposites.
Step 3: link each statement to a name or a number.
Step 4: repeat until all are named.
questions.tip: List → Pair → Link → Repeat.

similar.q: Why should keys use permanent, visible features?
similar.a: So anyone can check them on any specimen; colour or size may change with age.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

questions.q: A key for 12 organisms needs at least how many couplets?
why: Step 1: each couplet names one organism and passes the rest on.
Step 2: n organisms → n − 1 couplets.
questions.tip: n − 1 rule.

similar.q: How many couplets for 6 animals?
similar.a: 5 — as in the textbook key.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

questions.q: Which is the best couplet for a key?
why: Step 1: a couplet must be two opposite states of the same, visible feature.
Step 2: only “legs present / legs absent” is observable and mutually exclusive.
questions.tip: If two people could disagree on it, it is a bad couplet.

similar.q: Is “dangerous / harmless” a good couplet? Why?
similar.a: No — it is not a visible structural feature and people may disagree.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

questions.q: Turn couplet 2 of the textbook key into a question with its two answers.
questions.answer: Are wings present? Yes → the animal is a bat. No → go to couplet 3.
why: Step 1: take the feature (wings).
Step 2: ask “present?”
Step 3: give the Yes outcome (bat) and the No outcome (go to 3).
questions.tip: Every couplet becomes one yes/no question.

similar.q: Turn couplet 1 into a question.
similar.a: Is the animal aquatic and breathing with gills? Yes → fish. No → go to 2.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice

why: Step 1: prokaryote = no true nucleus.
Step 2: only bacteria and cyanobacteria lack a nucleus → Monera.
questions.tip: Monera = “no nucleus”.

similar.q: Name the two groups in kingdom Monera.
similar.a: Bacteria and cyanobacteria.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

questions.q: A plant cell wall is made of ____, while that of fungi is made of chitin.
why: Step 1: recall why fungi were separated from plants.
Step 2: walls differ chemically: plant = cellulose, fungi = chitin.
questions.tip: C for Cellulose and Chlorophyll (plants); chitin for fungi.

similar.q: Which kingdom has no cell wall?
similar.a: Animalia.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

questions.q: Compare the five kingdoms by cell type and nutrition.
questions.answer: Monera: prokaryotic; autotrophic or heterotrophic. Protista: eukaryotic, mostly unicellular; autotrophic (algae) or heterotrophic (protozoa, slime moulds). Fungi: eukaryotic; heterotrophic, absorb food. Plantae: eukaryotic multicellular; autotrophic (photosynthesis). Animalia: eukaryotic multicellular; heterotrophic, ingest food.
why: Step 1: cell type — only Monera prokaryotic; all others eukaryotic.
Step 2: nutrition — make (plants, algae, some monera), absorb (fungi), ingest (animals, protozoa).
Step 3: write one line per kingdom.
questions.tip: Use a table in the exam — it is faster and clearer.

similar.q: Which two kingdoms contain autotrophs that are eukaryotic?
similar.a: Protista (algae) and Plantae.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

why: Step 1: animals have no wall → A wrong.
Step 2: fungi absorb, not ingest → B wrong.
Step 3: plants have cellulose walls → C right.
Step 4: Monera have no true nucleus → D wrong.
questions.tip: Check each option against the kingdom table one by one.

similar.q: Which kingdom absorbs digested food?
similar.a: Fungi.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

questions.q: Viruses belong to kingdom Monera because they are very small.
why: Step 1: kingdoms group cellular organisms.
Step 2: viruses are not cells — DNA or RNA in a protein coat — and reproduce only inside host cells.
Step 3: they are not placed in any kingdom.
questions.tip: Small size is not a classification feature; cell structure is.

similar.q: Name two features that make viruses look non-living.
similar.a: They are not cells and they can be crystallised; no metabolism outside a host.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

questions.q: In the three-domain system, fungi, plants and animals are all placed in domain
why: Step 1: domains are Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
Step 2: fungi, plants and animals have eukaryotic cells → Eukarya.
questions.tip: Eu-karya = true nucleus.

similar.q: Which domains contain prokaryotes?
similar.a: Bacteria and Archaea.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice

questions.answer: The cell elongates; its chromosome duplicates; the cytoplasm divides into two and a new wall forms, giving two daughter cells, which grow and divide again every 20–30 minutes.
why: Step 1: elongate.
Step 2: duplicate DNA.
Step 3: divide cytoplasm and form a cross wall.
Step 4: two daughter cells, repeat in 20–30 min.
questions.tip: Grow → Copy → Split → Repeat.

similar.q: Name the primitive sexual process seen in *E. coli*.
similar.a: Conjugation — transfer of genetic material.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

questions.answer: Both make their own food (autotrophs). Photosynthetic bacteria use light energy; chemosynthetic bacteria use chemical energy from inorganic substances such as ammonia, hydrogen sulphide or hydrogen.
why: Step 1: same — both autotrophs, carbon from CO₂.
Step 2: different — energy source.
Step 3: photo = light; chemo = inorganic chemicals.
questions.tip: Always say what is the same before what is different.

similar.q: Nitrifying bacteria are examples of which type?
similar.a: Chemoautotrophs.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

questions.q: Organisms that obtain energy by oxidising inorganic chemicals are
why: Step 1: “inorganic” + make own food → autotroph.
Step 2: energy from chemicals, not light → chemoautotroph.
questions.tip: Chemo = chemicals.

similar.q: What do photoautotrophs use for energy?
similar.a: Light.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

questions.answer: In fragmentation a filament breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new organism. Example: filamentous cyanobacteria.
why: Step 1: define — breaking into fragments.
Step 2: each fragment grows into a new individual (asexual).
Step 3: example — cyanobacteria filaments (sponges also fragment).
questions.tip: Define + example = full marks.

similar.q: Do cyanobacteria reproduce sexually?
similar.a: No — only by cell division or fragmentation.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

why: Step 1: they lack flagella → A wrong.
Step 2: they photosynthesise like plants and release O₂ → B right.
Step 3: prokaryotes, no true nucleus → C wrong; asexual only → D wrong.
questions.tip: Cyano = blue; think “blue-green, gives O₂”.

similar.q: What else can many cyanobacteria fix from the air?
similar.a: Nitrogen.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

why: Step 1: sapro = rotten/dead.
Step 2: saprophytes feed on dead matter and waste → decomposers.
questions.tip: Sapro = dead, para = beside a living host.

similar.q: What do parasitic bacteria feed on?
similar.a: A living host.

questions.label: 2.3.1 Practice

questions.q: What feature identifies a protist as plant-like, animal-like or fungus-like?
questions.answer: Its mode of nutrition: plant-like protists (algae) photosynthesise; animal-like protists (protozoa) ingest food; fungus-like protists (slime moulds) absorb food.
why: Step 1: the three groups are split by nutrition.
Step 2: make food → algae.
Step 3: ingest → protozoa.
Step 4: absorb → slime moulds.
questions.tip: Make / Ingest / Absorb.

similar.q: Which group does *Euglena* belong to?
similar.a: Plant-like protists (algae).

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

questions.q: What type of protist is *Paramecium*? Give its distinguishing characteristics.
questions.answer: Animal-like protist (phylum Ciliophora). Covered by rows of cilia; oral groove leading to mouth pore and gullet; a small micronucleus and a large macronucleus; two contractile vacuoles; binary fission and conjugation.
why: Step 1: movement by cilia → Ciliophora (protozoa).
Step 2: list structures — cilia, oral groove, two nuclei, two contractile vacuoles.
Step 3: reproduction — binary fission, conjugation.
questions.tip: Give at least three structures for “distinguishing characteristics”.

similar.q: What is the role of the contractile vacuole?
similar.a: Removes excess water from the cytoplasm.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

questions.answer: It causes African sleeping sickness, spread by the tsetse fly: irregular fever, swelling and skin eruptions, then headache, convulsions, coma and death; first in the blood, later in the nervous system.
why: Step 1: name the disease.
Step 2: name the vector — tsetse fly.
Step 3: list symptoms in order.
questions.tip: Disease + vector + symptoms.

similar.q: Which protist causes amoebic dysentery?
similar.a: *Entamoeba histolytica*.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

why: Step 1: *P. vivax* — benign (mild), every 48 h.
Step 2: *P. falciparum* — malignant (harmful), every 36–48 h.
questions.tip: Falciparum = fatal-ciparum.

similar.q: Which two Plasmodium species are common in Eritrea?
similar.a: *P. vivax* and *P. falciparum*.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

questions.q: *Chlamydomonas* is an example of a unicellular ____ green alga.
why: Step 1: *Chlamydomonas* has two flagella.
Step 2: two flagella = biflagellate.
questions.tip: Bi = two.

similar.q: Which green alga is filamentous with a spiral chloroplast?
similar.a: *Spirogyra*.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

questions.q: The thick-walled structure formed after conjugation in *Spirogyra* is the
why: Step 1: conjugation → nuclei fuse → zygote.
Step 2: zygote gets a thick coat → zygospore.
questions.tip: Zygote + spore = zygospore.

similar.q: What anchors *Ulva* to the sea floor?
similar.a: A holdfast.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

options.B: are the primary food source of aquatic animals

why: Step 1: phytoplankton = photosynthetic unicellular algae in plankton.
Step 2: they make food that aquatic animals eat → primary food source.
questions.tip: Phyto = plant: producers.

similar.q: What are zooplankton?
similar.a: The tiny animals of the plankton.

questions.label: 2.3.2 Practice

questions.q: List the common characteristics of fungi.
questions.answer: Eukaryotic; mostly filamentous (hyphae forming a mycelium), some unicellular (yeast); cell walls of chitin; no chlorophyll; heterotrophic — secrete enzymes and absorb food (saprophytes, parasites or partners in lichens); reproduce by non-motile spores, sexually and asexually; important decomposers.
why: Step 1: structure — hyphae, mycelium, chitin.
Step 2: nutrition — no chlorophyll, absorb.
Step 3: reproduction — spores.
Step 4: role — decomposers.
questions.tip: Structure, Nutrition, Reproduction, Role — four headings.

similar.q: Give one distinguishing feature of Basidiomycota.
similar.a: Spores on a club-shaped basidium, four basidiospores each.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

why: Step 1: *Rhizopus* = black bread mould.
Step 2: hyphae without cross walls; sexual reproduction by conjugation → zygosporangium → Zygomycota.
questions.tip: Zebras Always Bite Donkeys: Z for Rhizopus.

similar.q: To which phylum does yeast belong?
similar.a: Ascomycota.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: An ascus of a typical sac fungus contains
why: Step 1: ascus = sac (Ascomycota).
Step 2: each ascus usually holds eight ascospores (yeast forms four).
questions.tip: Sac 8, club 4.

similar.q: How many spores does a basidium carry?
similar.a: Four basidiospores.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: Describe the fungal and algal association in a lichen.
questions.answer: Mutualism: the fungus holds water to keep the alga moist, digests the rock to release minerals and protects the alga; the alga photosynthesises and makes food for both.
why: Step 1: name the relationship — mutualism (both benefit).
Step 2: fungus gives water, minerals, protection.
Step 3: alga gives food by photosynthesis.
questions.tip: Say what EACH partner gives.

similar.q: What is mutualism?
similar.a: A symbiosis in which both partners benefit.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: How do fungal pathogens affect the way people live?
questions.answer: They cause human diseases (thrush by *Candida albicans*; ringworm and athlete’s foot by dermatophytes) and crop diseases (blight in potatoes and tomatoes; rust in wheat, barley and oats; downy mildew), causing great economic losses for farmers.
why: Step 1: human health examples.
Step 2: crop examples.
Step 3: consequence — food loss, money loss.
questions.tip: Two human + two crop examples is a strong answer.

similar.q: Name a useful product of fungi.
similar.a: Penicillin, bread, beer, wine, edible mushrooms.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: Deuteromycota are fungi in which sexual reproduction is unknown.
why: Step 1: deutero = “imperfect fungi”.
Step 2: called imperfect because no sexual stage is known.
Step 3: when one is found, they are moved to Ascomycota or Basidiomycota.
questions.tip: Imperfect = missing the sexual “perfect” stage.

similar.q: What happens when a sexual stage is discovered?
similar.a: The fungus is moved to Ascomycota or Basidiomycota.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: List three differences between fungi and plants.
questions.answer: Fungi: chitin walls, no chlorophyll, absorb food (heterotrophic), body of hyphae. Plants: cellulose walls, chlorophyll, photosynthesis (autotrophic), roots, stems and leaves.
why: Step 1: wall chemistry.
Step 2: chlorophyll and nutrition.
Step 3: body structure or food store.
questions.tip: Write as pairs: “Fungi …, whereas plants …”.

similar.q: Why were fungi once placed with plants?
similar.a: Because they have cell walls.

questions.label: 2.3.3 Practice

questions.q: Describe the life cycle of plants (alternation of generations).
questions.answer: The sporophyte produces spores; a spore grows into a gametophyte; the gametophyte produces gametes; two gametes fuse to form a zygote; the zygote grows into a new sporophyte.
why: Step 1: sporophyte → spores.
Step 2: spore → gametophyte.
Step 3: gametophyte → gametes.
Step 4: gametes fuse → zygote → sporophyte.
questions.tip: Draw it as a circle with four arrows.

similar.q: Which generation is dominant in ferns?
similar.a: The sporophyte.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

questions.q: What are the general characteristics of pteridophytes?
questions.answer: Seedless vascular plants (ferns, club mosses, horsetails) with true roots, stems and leaves; underground rhizome; leaves called fronds; reproduce by spores; dominant sporophyte; independent heart-shaped gametophyte (prothallus).
why: Step 1: vascular but seedless.
Step 2: true organs; rhizome; fronds.
Step 3: life cycle — dominant sporophyte, independent prothallus.
questions.tip: Vascular + seedless are the two key words.

similar.q: What is a prothallus?
similar.a: The small heart-shaped gametophyte of a fern.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

questions.answer: Monocots: one cotyledon, parallel veins, flower parts in threes, fibrous roots, scattered vascular bundles (teff, maize). Dicots: two cotyledons, net veins, parts in fours or fives, tap root, bundles in a ring (beans, chickpeas).
why: Step 1: seed — 1 vs 2 cotyledons.
Step 2: leaf veins.
Step 3: flower parts.
Step 4: roots and vascular bundles.
questions.tip: Use a two-column table.

similar.q: Is sorghum a monocot or dicot?
similar.a: Monocot.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

questions.q: In mosses, spores are produced inside the
why: Step 1: the moss sporophyte grows on the gametophyte.
Step 2: its tip is a capsule that releases spores.
Step 3: sori are on fern fronds.
questions.tip: Moss → capsule; fern → sori.

similar.q: Where are spores produced in a fern?
similar.a: In sori on the underside of the frond.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

questions.q: In angiosperms the seed is enclosed in a fruit that develops from the
why: Step 1: seeds develop in the ovary at the base of the flower.
Step 2: the ovary wall matures into the fruit.
questions.tip: Angio = vessel/case: seed in a case.

similar.q: How many species of flowering plants are there?
similar.a: More than 250 000.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

questions.q: Which plant group has seeds but no flowers?
why: Step 1: bryophytes and pteridophytes — no seeds.
Step 2: angiosperms — seeds and flowers.
Step 3: gymnosperms — naked seeds on cones, no flowers.
questions.tip: Brave Pupils Get A’s — seeds start at G, flowers at A.

similar.q: Name the two kinds of pine cones.
similar.a: Staminate (male, small) and ovulate (female, large) cones.

questions.label: 2.3.4 Practice

why: Step 1: jellyfish and starfish — radial.
Step 2: earthworms — bilateral.
Step 3: sponges — no symmetry.
questions.tip: Simplest animal = no symmetry.

similar.q: Name two radially symmetrical phyla.
similar.a: Cnidaria and Echinodermata.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: The stinging cells of cnidarians are
why: Step 1: spicules — sponge needles.
Step 2: setae — annelid bristles.
Step 3: choanocytes — sponge collar cells.
Step 4: nematocysts — cnidarian stinging cells on tentacles.
questions.tip: Nemato-cyst: sting “thread capsule”.

similar.q: Name the two body forms of cnidarians.
similar.a: Polyp and medusa.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: Why does a tapeworm not need a digestive system?
questions.answer: It lives in the host’s intestine, surrounded by food the host has already digested, and absorbs these soluble nutrients through its body surface.
why: Step 1: where it lives — intestine.
Step 2: what surrounds it — digested food.
Step 3: how it feeds — absorbs through body surface.
questions.tip: Habitat explains structure.

similar.q: What is the scolex for?
similar.a: Attachment to the host’s gut.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: Which group of arthropods has four pairs of legs and no antennae?
why: Step 1: four pairs = 8 legs.
Step 2: no antennae, cephalothorax + abdomen → arachnids (spiders, scorpions, ticks, mites).
questions.tip: 8 legs like the 8 letters in “arachnid”? Count: a-r-a-c-h-n-i-d = 8!

similar.q: How many pairs of antennae do crustaceans have?
similar.a: Two pairs.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: Distinguish complete and incomplete metamorphosis with examples.
questions.answer: Incomplete: egg → nymph → adult (three stages), e.g. grasshopper. Complete: egg → larva → pupa → adult (four stages), e.g. butterfly, house fly.
why: Step 1: define metamorphosis — marked change of form during growth.
Step 2: incomplete — 3 stages, nymph.
Step 3: complete — 4 stages, larva and pupa.
questions.tip: Pupa present = complete.

similar.q: In which type do young look like small adults?
similar.a: Incomplete (nymphs).

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: The water vascular system is found in
why: Step 1: unique to echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins).
Step 2: used in feeding, locomotion, respiration, sensing.
questions.tip: Echino = spiny skin, water feet.

similar.q: Do echinoderms have a brain?
similar.a: No — no head, eyes or brain.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: The part of a mollusc that secretes the shell is the
why: Step 1: foot — movement; radula — scraping; visceral mass — organs.
Step 2: mantle — fold over the visceral mass that secretes the shell.
questions.tip: Mantle = a coat that builds the shell.

similar.q: What is a radula?
similar.a: A toothed structure for scraping food or rock.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Invertebrates practice

questions.q: How do vertebrates differ from other animals?
questions.answer: They have a true, usually bony, endoskeleton with a backbone around the spinal cord and a skull around the brain; invertebrates have no backbone.
why: Step 1: name the key structure — backbone.
Step 2: add skull and endoskeleton.
questions.tip: Back-bone + brain-box (skull).

similar.q: Name the five vertebrate classes.
similar.a: Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: Explain why reptiles were among the first vertebrates fully adapted to land.
questions.answer: Dry waterproof scaly skin reduces water loss; they breathe only by lungs; fertilisation is internal; eggs have shells, so they do not need water to reproduce.
why: Step 1: water loss — scaly skin.
Step 2: breathing — lungs.
Step 3: reproduction — internal fertilisation, shelled eggs.
questions.tip: Skin, lungs, eggs — three points.

similar.q: Why must frogs return to water to breed?
similar.a: External fertilisation and eggs without shells; tadpoles live in water.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: Differentiate between internal and external fertilisation.
questions.answer: External: sperm and eggs fuse outside the female’s body, usually in water (most fishes, frogs). Internal: fusion inside the female’s body (sharks, reptiles, birds, mammals).
why: Step 1: define each by where the gametes meet.
Step 2: give examples of each.
questions.tip: Out = water animals, In = land animals (mostly).

similar.q: Which fish uses internal fertilisation?
similar.a: Sharks.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: Which feature is unique to birds?
why: Step 1: mammals also have four chambers and are warm-blooded.
Step 2: reptiles and monotremes lay eggs.
Step 3: only birds have feathers.
questions.tip: “Unique” = no other class has it.

similar.q: Give three functions of feathers.
similar.a: Insulation, flight, waterproofing (also UV protection, colour).

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: The kangaroo is an example of a
why: Step 1: monotremes lay eggs (platypus).
Step 2: marsupials have a short placenta then a pouch → kangaroo.
questions.tip: Marsupial = pouch.

similar.q: Name an egg-laying mammal.
similar.a: Platypus or spiny anteater.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: Fishes are animals with a variable body temperature, known as ____.
why: Step 1: variable temperature = cold-blooded.
Step 2: the term is poikilothermic.
questions.tip: Poikilo = changing.

similar.q: What are animals with a constant body temperature called?
similar.a: Homoeothermic.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: An animal with long, flat grinding teeth is most likely a
why: Step 1: teeth match diet.
Step 2: grinding plant material needs flat teeth → herbivore.
questions.tip: Look at teeth → know the diet.

similar.q: Give two examples of omnivorous mammals.
similar.a: Humans and pigs.

questions.label: 2.3.5 Vertebrates practice

questions.q: Who is known as the father of modern taxonomy?
why: Answer C: Carl Linnaeus.
Linnaeus built the hierarchy of ranks and binomial nomenclature.
Whittaker proposed the five kingdoms; Hooke named cells.
questions.tip: Linnaeus = Latin names.

similar.q: Who proposed the five-kingdom system?
similar.a: R. H. Whittaker (1969).

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: The correct sequence of taxa from highest to lowest is

options.A: Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Family, Genus, Species
options.B: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
options.C: Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Genus, Family, Species
options.D: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom

Use King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
D is the reverse order (lowest to highest).
questions.tip: Read the question: highest → lowest.

similar.q: Which rank is directly below kingdom?
similar.a: Phylum.

questions.q: The scientific name of any organism consists of
why: Answer D: genus and species.
Binomial = two names: genus + species.
questions.tip: Bi-nomial = two names.

similar.q: Which part of *Felis leo* is the genus?
similar.a: *Felis*.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: Which of the following organisms are most closely related?

options.A: Two members of the same family
options.B: Two members of the same order
options.C: Two members of the same genus
options.D: Two members of the same class

why: Answer C: Two members of the same genus.
The lower the shared rank, the closer the relationship.
Genus is the lowest rank among the options.
questions.tip: Lower shared rank = closer relatives.

similar.q: Are human and lion in the same order?
similar.a: No — Primates vs Carnivora; same class Mammalia.

similar.a: A couplet.

similar.q: Is *Amoeba* in the same kingdom?

They make food using chemical energy from oxidising ammonia.
questions.tip: Chemo = chemicals, auto = self-feeding.

similar.q: What do photoautotrophs use?
similar.a: Light energy.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: Cell division in bacteria takes place mainly by
why: Answer B: binary fission.
Bacteria split into two daughter cells every 20–30 minutes.
Conjugation is genetic transfer, not division.
questions.tip: Binary = two.

similar.q: How many bacteria from one after 2 hours if it divides every 30 min?

Cyanobacteria produced the first oxygen; decomposers recycle minerals; parasites cause disease.
questions.tip: When every option is true, choose “all of the above”.

similar.q: Which bacteria fix nitrogen and photosynthesise?
similar.a: Cyanobacteria.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: An organism with pseudopodia belongs to phylum
why: Answer C: Sarcodina.
Pseudopodia (false feet) are the locomotory structure of Sarcodina, e.g. *Amoeba*.
questions.tip: Sarco walks on false feet.

similar.q: Which phylum moves by flagella?
similar.a: Mastigophora.

*Trypanosoma* → sleeping sickness → tsetse fly.
Anopheles carries Plasmodium.
questions.tip: Match parasite → disease → vector in a chain.

similar.a: The female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: Which of the following is a colonial green alga?
why: Answer C: *Volvox*.
*Chlamydomonas* unicellular, *Spirogyra* filamentous, *Ulva* multicellular, *Volvox* colonial.
questions.tip: Volvox = a “village” of cells.

similar.q: Which green alga is two cells thick with a holdfast?
similar.a: *Ulva* (sea lettuce).

questions.q: Fungi are very important in the environment as
why: Answer B: decomposers.

questions.tip: Saprophyte → decomposer.

similar.q: What is a mass of hyphae called?
similar.a: Mycelium.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: The fungus and alga in a lichen live in a relationship called
why: Answer C: mutualism.
Both partners benefit → mutualism.
questions.tip: Mutual = both.

similar.q: What does the alga give the fungus?
similar.a: Food made by photosynthesis.

why: Answer B: basidia.
Basidiomycota = club fungi; basidium bears four basidiospores.
questions.tip: Sac 8 (ascus), club 4 (basidium).

similar.q: In which phylum is yeast?
similar.a: Ascomycota.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a fungus?
why: Answer C: Athlete’s foot.
Malaria, sleeping sickness and amoebic dysentery are caused by protozoa.
Athlete’s foot is caused by dermatophyte fungi.
questions.tip: Protozoa: malaria, sleeping sickness, dysentery; fungi: thrush, ringworm, athlete’s foot.

similar.q: Which fungus causes thrush?
similar.a: *Candida albicans*.

why: Answer B: capsule.
The moss sporophyte ends in a capsule that releases spores.

similar.a: The gametophyte.

Plants are classified by presence or absence of vessels and seeds.

similar.a: Pteridophytes (ferns).

Cnidarians (*Hydra*, jellyfish) are radial; the others are bilateral.

similar.q: Which phylum is asymmetrical?

questions.tip: Clitellum → cocoon.

similar.q: What helps earthworms anchor during movement?
similar.a: Setae.

Osteo = bone.
Rays and skates are cartilaginous; bony fishes have jaws.
questions.tip: Osteo = bone, chondro = cartilage.

similar.q: What gives bony fishes buoyancy?
similar.a: The swim bladder.

questions.label: Unit exercise (matric style)

questions.q: Which arthropod group has three body parts and three pairs of legs?
why: Answer C: Insects.
Insects: head, thorax, abdomen; 3 pairs of legs on the thorax.

similar.q: How many legs does a spider have?
similar.a: Eight.

similar.q: What is a virus made of?

similar.q: What would net veins and two cotyledons indicate?
similar.a: A dicot.

why: Answer A: Yeast and mushroom.

Amoeba and Paramecium ingest food; mosses, ferns, Euglena, Volvox photosynthesise.

Polyp = attached, mouth up; medusa = free-floating, mouth down. The planula is the larva.

similar.q: What is the swimming larva of cnidarians called?
similar.a: Planula.

units.intro: **Biomolecules:** carbohydrates (sugars, starch, cellulose — C,H,O; energy and plant walls), lipids (fats/oils — energy store, membranes), proteins (amino acids — enzymes, structure), nucleic acids (DNA/RNA — information).

cards.title: 3.1.1 Carbohydrates
body: **Carbohydrates** are the most abundant organic compounds in living organisms.
Based on the sugar units they contain, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, disaccharides or polysaccharides.
Carbohydrates are mainly found in plants such as potatoes, rice and wheat.
Monosaccharides are single sugar containing molecules.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Lipids
body: The word lipid comes from the Greek word “lipos”, meaning “fat” or “lard” (fat of pork/a pig).
Like carbohydrates, lipids are large molecules made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The most common lipids are fats, oils and waxes.
Lipids are found in animals and plants e.g. butter and groundnut oil.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Proteins
body: Protein molecules are made up of long chains of smaller molecules joined end to end.
Amino acids are classified as essential or non-essential amino acids.
Essential amino acids are those which cannot be synthesized by the body.
Non-essential amino acids are those that the body can synthesize from other amino acids or nutrients present in food.

cards.title: 3.1.4 Nucleic acids
body: The two nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) vary in some of their structural components and in their functions.

cards.title: 3.2 The Energy Flow in Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration
body: **Photosynthesis** is a chemical process that takes place in plants to make food.
Green plants use solar energy to make biomolecules.
Most plants have a green substance, called chlorophyll, found inside the chloroplasts of plant cells.
Plants get carbon dioxide from the air, whereas water is absorbed from the soil by their root hairs.
Photosynthesis occurs in two reactions, called a light reaction and a dark reaction.

cards.title: Formula
body: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Light + chlorophyll. Respiration is the reverse energy story: glucose broken to release ATP.

cards.title: Step by step: Energy flow in photosynthesis and respiration
body: **Step 1:** Photosynthesis traps light energy using chlorophyll in chloroplasts: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light energy → chemical energy in glucose).
**Step 2:** Light-dependent stage: light splits water, releasing O₂ and making ATP and NADPH.
**Step 3:** Light-independent stage (Calvin cycle): CO₂ is fixed into glucose using the ATP and NADPH.
**Step 4:** Respiration in the mitochondria releases the energy in glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP).
**Step 5:** The two processes form a cycle: the products of one are the raw materials of the other; energy flows one way (Sun → glucose → ATP → heat) while matter is recycled.
**Example:** A plant in sunlight takes in CO₂ and gives out O₂ because photosynthesis is faster than respiration; at night it only respires, so it takes in O₂ and gives out CO₂.

units.intro:
**Adaptation** is a feature that helps survival and reproduction in a habitat. Not “the animal wanted it.”

**Plants:** cold — short season, dwarf, dark leaves sometimes. Drought — small/waxy leaves, sunken stomata, deep or wide roots, water store (cactus). Salt — salt glands, succulence. Wind — flexible stems, small leaves. Eritrea highland vs coastal desert is the local pair to use in essays.

cards.title: 4.1 What is Adaptation?
body: Living organisms are characterized by the changes they make to live in the environmental conditions around them.
The changes can be morphological (change in structure and form) or physiological (internal and functional change), and is called **adaptation**.
**Adaptation** is the modification in structure or function that increases the fitness of an organism in a stressful environment.
Adaptation is hereditary and thus passed from one generation to the next.
Adaptation mechanisms of living organisms to various environmental stress factors are generally classified as avoidance, tolerance and escape mechanisms.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Adaptations of Plants to Temperature
body: **Temperature** is a very important environmental factor that affects plant functions and growth.
At low temperatures, plants develop adaptations that allow them to reduce their exposure to the cold environment.
**Transpiration** is the loss of water from plants through the small openings called stomata in the leaves and stems.
The low temperature limits soil water uptake.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Adaptations of Plants to Water
body: Plants are classified into three major categories according to their adaptations to water conditions.
The majority of plant species live in optimal environments with regard to water availability.
Mesophytes are plants that live under normal water conditions or in intermediate water availability e.g. many crop species.
Mesophytes usually have a well developed root system, their leaves are flat and their stomata do not have protective features.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Adaptations of Plants to Salt
body: Plants such as mangroves, that cover a great part of the seashores in Massawa and the coastal areas, are salt-tolerant plants.
Mangroves also have small openings (lenticels) in their bark that allow oxygen to diffuse into the plant and down into its underground roots.
Many salt-tolerant plants have developed salt glands, salt-filtering root, or salt-excreting leaves or branches in order to prevent the build up of high salt concentrations.
Mangroves for example almost completely eliminate salt and, when squeezed, their leaves consist of almost pure water.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Adaptations of Animals to Low Temperatures
body: The ear size of goats living in cold regions is smaller than that of goats living in warm regions.
Hormonal changes: In cold weather hormonal changes tend to boost the metabolic rate.
Insulation: A major thermoregulatory adaptation in mammals and birds is insulation.
Mammals develop hair (often called fur), or have fat deposits in their bodies.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Adaptations of Animals to High Temperatures
body: Aestivation: In regions where the day-time temperature is very high and the water supply is very scarce, some animals tolerate (endure) the period of high temperature by aestivation.
Nocturnal behaviour: There are many animals that become active and feed during the night, becoming inactive during the day e.g. bats.

cards.title: Explaining an animal adaptation
cards.problem: Explain three ways in which a polar bear is adapted to the cold Arctic environment.

steps.text: Identify the problem: very low temperatures cause heat loss.
Adaptation 1: thick fur and a thick layer of fat (blubber) under the skin insulate the body and reduce heat loss.
Adaptation 2: small ears and a large body give a small surface area to volume ratio, so less heat is lost.
Adaptation 3: white fur camouflages it against snow for hunting; wide, furry paws spread its weight on ice.

cards.answer: Thick fur and blubber (insulation), small surface area to volume ratio (less heat loss), and white fur / wide paws (camouflage, walking on ice).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are true about adaptation of animals to **high temperature**, **except**
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Analyze heat adaptations. Aestivation (summer sleep), nocturnal activity, lack of insulating fat, and large ears (for cooling) are all heat adaptations.
**Step 2:** **Hibernation** (winter sleep) is a state of inactivity and metabolic depression in endotherms to survive cold temperatures and food scarcity.
**Step 3:** Therefore, hibernation is not an adaptation to high temperature.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which adaptation helps a camel survive in the desert?

options.A: It has a thick layer of fat all over its body
options.B: It sweats heavily at low temperatures
options.D: It produces very concentrated urine and dry faeces

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Deserts are hot and dry, so saving water is vital.

**Step 2:** Camels lose very little water in urine and faeces and can tolerate large rises in body temperature before sweating.

**Step 3:** The hump stores fat in one place, so the rest of the body loses heat easily; wide feet stop sinking in sand.

**Tip:** Explain each adaptation with its benefit ("…so that less water is lost").

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Gills absorb dissolved oxygen from water.

**Step 2:** A streamlined body reduces water resistance; fins help balance and steering.

**Step 3:** Answer: gills and a streamlined body.

**Tip:** In exam answers link each structure to the problem of living in water (getting O₂, moving easily).
